items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] ...Like David Baker talks about he teaches people what you have contributed to the music.

ctx.x: Composer David Baker talks about the neglect of this music; the carelessness evident in documenting this music and putting it on good terms with others of the world's great musics. This is so perhaps because ignorance and inaccurate historical attention. It is so perhaps because of the growth of the world and the many uses of the music which obscure its origins and continuity in its original culture. It is so.
We will be talking at length with Mr. Ware, considered by his contemporaries and followers as a primary American bass innovator.

items.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview
items.q: You know, like Dave Baker was telling us?

ctx.x: I noticed you were talking about, towards the end, the college dates that people are working, that you were working with Monk. There seemed to be a trend more in the '70s.

It is. The college kids are very aware of what had been before them. They didn't get a chance to hear it like we did as high school kids because it's not in the theaters like it used to be. So most of the concerts they do see, they have to go to New York to catch the Newport things or some big concert. They only see one side of it, whoever the promoter is pushing, you know. They don't see people that they've been hearing about for years.

So, they're running courses on it. The colleges are hiring people, you know, artists in residence, to bring the music to them. They are eating it up. They are really getting into it. You know, like Dave Baker was telling us?
